segments.title: Raptor: The Engine That Makes Starship Possible
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about the evolution of SpaceX's Raptor engine. Cover why full-flow staged combustion matters (efficiency, chamber pressure, turbine longevity), the methalox propellant choice and its link to Mars in-situ propellant production, and the progression from Raptor 1 through Raptor 3 — fewer parts, less external plumbing, higher thrust, lower cost per engine. Explain the manufacturing-rate story: Raptor is designed to be mass-produced like a car part, not hand-built like a traditional rocket engine.

segments.title: The Heat Shield Problem: Starship's Hardest Engineering Challenge
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about Starship's thermal protection system. Cover why rapid-reuse reentry is harder than expendable reentry, the hexagonal ceramic tile approach versus the Shuttle's bespoke tiles, the attachment and gap-filler failure modes seen on test flights, ablative backup layers, and why a fully reusable heat shield that needs zero refurbishment between flights is the single biggest unsolved engineering problem standing between Starship and airline-like operations.

segments.title: Falcon 9 Reuse Economics: What a Flight-Proven Booster Really Saves
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about the economics of Falcon 9 booster reuse. Cover the rough cost structure of a Falcon 9 launch (booster, upper stage, fairings, propellant, operations), what refurbishment between flights actually involves, how fleet-leader boosters have pushed past their original design life, fairing recovery, and how reuse enabled both the Starlink build-out and price leadership in the commercial launch market. Use real numbers where possible and be honest about what SpaceX has and hasn't disclosed.

segments.title: Starlink by the Numbers: Constellation Design and Capacity Economics
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about Starlink's constellation architecture. Cover the orbital shell design and why low altitude matters for latency and debris self-cleaning, inter-satellite laser links, the satellite generations and how launch mass drives Starship dependency, direct-to-cell service, and the capacity economics — why bandwidth per cell, not subscriber count alone, determines Starlink's revenue ceiling. Explain how Starlink became the revenue engine that funds Starship development.

segments.title: Stage Zero: The Launch Pad as a Machine
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about SpaceX's launch infrastructure — what the company calls 'Stage Zero'. Cover the orbital launch mount, the tower catch ('Mechazilla' chopstick) approach and why catching a booster beats landing legs for rapid reuse, the tank farm and propellant logistics of loading thousands of tonnes of methalox, the water deluge system, and pad turnaround as a launch-cadence bottleneck. Explain why SpaceX treats the pad as flight hardware that iterates as fast as the rocket.

segments.title: Orbital Refueling: The Make-or-Break Technology
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about orbital propellant transfer. Explain why Starship's deep-space ambitions (the Moon via Artemis HLS, Mars) depend on ship-to-ship cryogenic propellant transfer in orbit, the physics challenges — propellant settling, boiloff, docking and fluid connections in microgravity — the tanker flight cadence a single lunar landing requires, and what has been demonstrated so far versus what remains. Be honest about the timeline risk this places on Artemis.

segments.title: Starshield: SpaceX's Quiet Defense Business
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about Starshield, SpaceX's national-security satellite line. Cover how Starshield differs from Starlink (government-controlled payloads, encryption, hosted sensors), the known contracts and their strategic significance, how proliferated LEO constellations change military space architecture away from a few exquisite satellites, and the questions this business raises — revenue concentration, dual-use policy tensions, and what investors can and cannot learn from public disclosures.

segments.title: Why SpaceX Builds Almost Everything In-House
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about SpaceX's vertical integration philosophy. Cover the stainless-steel switch for Starship (cost per kilogram, weldability, thermal properties versus carbon fiber), in-house avionics and flight computers, engine production rates traditional aerospace considered impossible, and the 'the best part is no part' design ethos. Contrast with the traditional aerospace prime-and-subcontractor model and explain the trade-offs: capital intensity and single-company risk versus iteration speed and cost control.

segments.title: The Musk Compute Stack: How xAI and SpaceX Interlock
segments.prompt_template: Write a deep-dive segment about the relationship between SpaceX and the broader Musk AI-and-compute ecosystem — xAI, Grok, the Colossus data center build-out, and the emerging orbital-compute thesis. Cover the concrete, verifiable links (Starlink connectivity for data centers, Starshield hosting, launch capacity for AI-relevant payloads, shared engineering culture) and clearly separate them from speculative ones (orbital data centers, space-based inference). Explain what the AI & Compute thread means for how investors think about SPCX.

segments.title: Four Flights from Bankruptcy: The Falcon 1 Story
segments.prompt_template: Write a historical perspective segment about Falcon 1 and SpaceX's near-death in 2008. Cover the three consecutive failures and their specific engineering causes (fuel line corrosion at Kwajalein, stage recontact after the Merlin upgrade), the company having funding for essentially one more attempt, flight 4's success in September 2008, and the NASA CRS contract that saved the company weeks later. Draw out the engineering-culture lessons — flying to learn, root-causing fast — that still define SpaceX today.

segments.title: Sticking the Landing: From Grasshopper to the Drone Ship
segments.prompt_template: Write a historical perspective segment tracing SpaceX's decade-long quest to land an orbital-class booster. Cover the Grasshopper and F9R test hops, the ocean 'landings', the barge crashes and what each failure taught (grid fins, throttle authority, stiction in the landing legs), the first land landing in December 2015 and the first drone-ship landing on CRS-8 in April 2016. Explain why propulsive landing of an orbital booster was considered impossible by much of the industry, and how routine it became.

segments.title: Commercial Crew: How Fixed-Price Contracts Changed Spaceflight
segments.prompt_template: Write a historical perspective segment about SpaceX's path through NASA's COTS and Commercial Crew programs. Cover the shift from cost-plus to fixed-price milestone contracts, Dragon's cargo years, the Demo-2 crewed flight in 2020 ending America's reliance on Soyuz, and the instructive contrast with Boeing's Starliner program on both schedule and cost. Explain how the commercial model transferred design ownership to the contractor and what that has meant for NASA's approach since.

segments.title: Starlink's Ceiling: Bull and Bear on the Revenue Engine
segments.prompt_template: Write a balanced contrarian segment on Starlink's growth ceiling. The bull case: global addressable market for connectivity, direct-to-cell, aviation and maritime, government demand. The bear case: subscriber saturation in high-income rural markets, capacity constraints in dense areas, Amazon's Kuiper and Chinese constellations arriving, terminal subsidy economics, and regulatory friction in large markets. Present both sides fairly with real numbers where available and let the listener decide.

segments.title: The Mars Question: Vision, Business Plan, or Both?
segments.prompt_template: Write a balanced contrarian segment about the economics of Mars settlement. One side: Mars as the mission that recruits world-class engineers, forces full reusability, and produced the most valuable launch company on Earth as a by-product — the vision IS the business model. The other side: no credible revenue exists on Mars, settlement costs are staggering, and shareholder capital may subsidize a goal with no return horizon. Discuss how a public SPCX balances mission and fiduciary duty. Be fair to both sides.

segments.title: How to Read a Launch Manifest Like an Analyst
segments.prompt_template: Write a practical utility segment teaching listeners how to interpret SpaceX launch-cadence data as a business signal. Cover what annual launch-count records do and don't tell you (internal Starlink flights versus external customer revenue), pad utilization across Florida and Vandenberg, booster fleet turnaround times as an operational-health metric, how scrubs and range conflicts distort weekly numbers, and where to find reliable public manifest data. Give listeners a simple mental checklist for separating cadence signal from noise.

segments.title: Evaluating SPCX: The Metrics That Actually Matter
segments.prompt_template: Write a practical utility segment on how to evaluate SpaceX as a public company. Cover the major revenue segments (launch services, Starlink consumer/enterprise, government and Starshield) and their very different margin profiles, the capital-expenditure story (Starship development, Starbase, satellite production), key disclosures to watch in public filings, and the honest uncertainties — how much of the valuation rests on Starship succeeding. Teach the framework, not a price target, and remind listeners this is not financial advice.

segments.title: Profile: Gwynne Shotwell
segments.prompt_template: Write a profile segment about Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's long-time President and COO. Cover her engineering background, joining SpaceX in 2002 as employee number 11 to lead sales, her role winning the NASA contracts that kept the company alive, how she runs day-to-day operations and customer relationships as the stabilizing counterpart to Elon Musk, and her influence on SpaceX's reputation for delivery. Explain why insiders often call her the most underrated executive in aerospace.

segments.title: Profile: Tom Mueller and the Merlin Engine
segments.prompt_template: Write a profile segment about Tom Mueller, SpaceX's founding propulsion engineer. Cover his path from Idaho logger's son and amateur rocketry champion to TRW propulsion engineer, becoming SpaceX employee number one on the technical side, designing the Merlin engine family that powers Falcon 9, laying the groundwork for Raptor, and his post-SpaceX venture Impulse Space. Explain how Merlin's simplicity-first design philosophy shaped everything SpaceX built afterward.
